claim: Protein aggregates are spatially organized and regulated in cells to prevent the deleterious effects of proteostatic stress.
source: Protein aggregates are spatially organized and regulated in cells to prevent the deleterious effects of proteostatic stress.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding about protein aggregate regulation.

claim: Misfolding of proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) results in aggregate formation.
source: Misfolding of proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) results in aggregate formation, but how the aggregates are processed, especially during cell division is not well understood.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP forms solid-like protein aggregates deposited mainly in the nucleus and surrounded by the ER membrane.
source: Unexpectedly, we detected solid-like protein aggregates deposited mainly in the nucleus and surrounded by the ER membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and detailed in the results section with microscopy data.

claim: Membrane-bound aggregates are cleared as cells progress through mitosis and cytokinesis.
source: The membrane-bound aggregates were then cleared as cells progressed through mitosis and cytokinesis.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing aggregate clearance during cell division.

claim: Aggregate clearance depends on Hsp70 family chaperones in the ER, particularly BiP.
source: Aggregate clearance depended on Hsp70 family chaperones in the ER, particularly BiP, and proteasomal activity.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using inhibitors of HSP70 and BiP ATPase activity.

claim: Aggregate clearance depends on proteasomal activity.
source: Aggregate clearance depended on Hsp70 family chaperones in the ER, particularly BiP, and proteasomal activity.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using proteasome inhibitor MG132.

claim: Aggregate clearance culminates at mitotic exit and requires cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (Cdk1) inactivation.
source: The clearance culminated at mitotic exit and required cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (Cdk1) inactivation but was independent of the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C).
evidence: This is supported by experiments using Cdk1 inhibitor RO-3306 in MG132-arrested cells.

claim: Aggregate clearance is independent of the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C).
source: The clearance culminated at mitotic exit and required cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (Cdk1) inactivation but was independent of the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C).
evidence: This is supported by experiments using APC/C inhibitors showing no effect on aggregate clearance.

claim: ER reorganization that is active during mitosis and cytokinesis is required for aggregate clearance.
source: The ER reorganization that is active during mitosis and cytokinesis was required for the aggregate clearance.
evidence: This is supported by experiments depleting ER membrane fusion proteins ATL2 and ATL3, and inhibiting Aurora A kinase.

claim: Misfolded proteins tend to have their hydrophobic residues exposed and result in aggregation of proteins.
source: Misfolded proteins tend to have their hydrophobic residues exposed and result in aggregation of proteins (Hartl et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hartl et al., 2011.

claim: Intramolecular beta-sheets in some proteins are structural elements prone to protein aggregation.
source: Intramolecular beta-sheets in some proteins are also structural elements prone to protein aggregation (Tyedmers et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tyedmers et al., 2010.

claim: Protein misfolding and aggregation can interfere with other proteins' functions by co-aggregation.
source: Protein misfolding and aggregation not only disrupt the native function of the protein but also could interfere with other proteins' functions by co-aggregation (Olzscha et al., 2011; Woerner et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Olzscha et al., 2011 and Woerner et al., 2016.

claim: Proteostatic stress is a main driver of cellular aging and neurodegenerative disorders.
source: This challenges proteome homeostasis (proteostasis) and causes proteostatic stress in cells, which is a main driver of cellular aging and neurodegenerative disorders (Balch et al., 2008; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Balch et al., 2008 and Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015.

claim: Molecular chaperones facilitate refolding, degradation, and spatial deposition of misfolded protein aggregates.
source: Cells evolve several protein quality control (PQC) systems to maintain their proteostasis in which components of PQC systems facilitate refolding, degradation, and spatial deposition of misfolded protein aggregates (Jayaraj et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jayaraj et al., 2020.

claim: Molecular chaperones are involved in folding nascent polypeptides, targeting misfolded proteins for degradation, and promoting solubilization of protein aggregates.
source: They are involved to fold nascent polypeptides, target misfolded proteins for degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system or autophagy, and promote solubilization of protein aggregates (Tyedmers et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tyedmers et al., 2010.

claim: Eukaryotic cells confine misfolded proteins and smaller aggregates into distinct cellular deposition sites.
source: Eukaryotic cells confine misfolded proteins and smaller aggregates into distinct cellular deposition sites, which reduce the reactivity of these harmful species to the proteome (Kaganovich et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kaganovich et al., 2008.

claim: Aggregate deposition sites include aggresomes, INQ, CytoQ, and IPOD.
source: These deposition sites include aggresomes or aggresome-like induced structures locating near centrosomes, INQ (intranuclear quality control compartment) residing in the nucleus, cytosolic CytoQ, and the perivacuolar IPOD (insoluble protein deposit) (Kaganovich et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kaganovich et al., 2008.

claim: Confinement of protein aggregates in a deposition site facilitates retention of aggregates in short-lived cells during asymmetric cell division.
source: Confinement of protein aggregates in a deposition site facilitates retention of aggregates in short-lived cells (mother cells) during asymmetric cell division (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Fuentealba et al., 2008; Rujano et al., 2006; Singhvi and Garriga, 2009; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies on asymmetric cell division.

claim: The ER processes one-third of cellular proteome.
source: The ER processes one-third of cellular proteome and possesses stronger ability to maintain aggregation-prone proteins in a non-toxic state than the cytosol owing to its specific molecular chaperone environment (Vincenz-Donnelly et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vincenz-Donnelly et al., 2018.

claim: The ER possesses stronger ability to maintain aggregation-prone proteins in a non-toxic state than the cytosol.
source: The ER processes one-third of cellular proteome and possesses stronger ability to maintain aggregation-prone proteins in a non-toxic state than the cytosol owing to its specific molecular chaperone environment (Vincenz-Donnelly et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vincenz-Donnelly et al., 2018.

claim: HSPA5/BiP regulates the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: Chaperones in the ER such as HSPA5/BiP regulates the unfolded protein response (UPR), which blocks instant protein synthesis and activates transcription of genes involved in PQC (Preissler and Ron, 2019; Wiseman et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Preissler and Ron, 2019 and Wiseman et al., 2022.

claim: Proteostatic stress in the ER triggers ER-associated degradation (ERAD) and ER-phagy to remove misfolded proteins.
source: In addition, the proteostatic stress in the ER triggers ER-associated degradation (ERAD) and ER-phagy to remove misfolded proteins (Mochida and Nakatogawa, 2022; Olzmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mochida and Nakatogawa, 2022 and Olzmann et al., 2013.

claim: Excessive misfolded proteins lead to formation of protein aggregates in the ER.
source: Despite the high capacity of proteostatic stress response in the ER (Rousseau et al., 2004; Vincenz-Donnelly et al., 2018), excessive misfolded proteins still lead to formation of protein aggregates in the ER (Melo et al., 2022; Miyata et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Melo et al., 2022 and Miyata et al., 2020.

claim: BiP functions as a disaggregase to promote solubilization of protein aggregates in the ER.
source: In response to protein aggregation in the ER, BiP functions as a disaggregase to promote solubilization of these aggregates.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about BiP function.

claim: The ER diffusion barrier and ERSU pathway ensure ER protein aggregates are retained preferentially in mother cells during asymmetric cell division in budding yeast.
source: In cells undergoing asymmetric cell division, such as in the budding yeast, the ER diffusion barrier and the ER stress surveillance (ERSU) pathway ensure ER protein aggregates are retained preferentially in the short-lived mother cells during cell division (Clay et al., 2014; Piña and Niwa, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Clay et al., 2014 and Piña and Niwa, 2015.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP assembled into visible protein aggregates in the nucleus when stably expressed in MCF10A cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that ER-FlucDM-eGFP assembled into visible protein aggregates in the nucleus when stably expressed in mammary epithelial MCF10A cells in the absence of any perturbation of the proteome stability (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1A showing aggregates in the nucleus.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP protein aggregates were below detection limit in the first 2 days after lentivirus transduction but progressively accumulated and stabilized several days after transduction.
source: The protein aggregates were below detection limit of our microscopy in the first 2 d after lentivirus transduction but progressively accumulated in cells and stabilized in the population several days after lentivirus transduction.
evidence: This is based on observations of cells at different time points after transduction.

claim: ER-FlucDM-mCherry localizes to the ER network as indicated by the ER membrane protein Sec61β.
source: ER-FlucDM-mCherry localized to the ER network indicated by the ER membrane protein Sec61β (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NLS-FlucDM-eGFP did not form protein aggregates in the nucleus.
source: Our data showed that NLS-FlucDM-eGFP did not form protein aggregates in the nucleus and was not co-localized with the ER-FlucDM-mCherry and accumulated lower protein abundance than ER-FlucDM-eGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and protein blotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: NLS-FlucDM-eGFP accumulated lower protein abundance than ER-FlucDM-eGFP.
source: Our data showed that NLS-FlucDM-eGFP did not form protein aggregates in the nucleus and was not co-localized with the ER-FlucDM-mCherry and accumulated lower protein abundance than ER-FlucDM-eGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by protein blotting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP has significantly reduced enzymatic activity compared to wild-type luciferase.
source: Luciferase activity measurement showed that ER-FlucDM-eGFP has significantly reduced enzymatic activity and was not functional possibly due to misfolding and protein aggregation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase activity assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP was detected in the insoluble fraction after heat stress.
source: ER-FlucDM-eGFP was also detected in the insoluble fraction after heat stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by protein fractionation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates colocalize with thioflavin T (ThT).
source: Moreover, we observed the colocalization of ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates and thioflavin T (ThT), a universal dye to detect amyloid fibrils, further supporting these aggregates were misfolded protein aggregates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP forms protein aggregates in the nucleus in multiple cell lines including A549, MDA-MB-231, and U2OS cells.
source: Formation of protein aggregates in the nucleus by ER-FlucDM-eGFP was not limited to MCF10A cells. The protein aggregates were also detected in the nucleus when ER-FlucDM-eGFP was expressed in other cell lines such as A549, MDA-MB-231, and U2OS cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: ER-HaloDM-eGFP forms protein aggregates in the nucleus similar to ER-FlucDM-eGFP.
source: In addition, when ER-FlucDM was replaced by ER-HaloDM, which is a modified haloalkane dehalogenase prone to misfolding and aggregation (Melo et al., 2022), we observed similar protein aggregates in the nucleus (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Only a very low number of cells formed aggregates in the nucleus when intact GFP was targeted to the ER.
source: However, only a very low number of cells formed aggregates in the nucleus when intact GFP was targeted to the ER (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP protein aggregates are surrounded by the ER membrane.
source: Despite localizing in the nucleus, we found that the protein aggregates were surrounded by the ER membrane as stained by the ER-tracker (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing colocalization with ER-tracker in Figure 1E.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates are surrounded by a single-layer membrane close to the inner membrane of the nucleus.
source: We found that the aggregates were surrounded by a single-layer membrane closed to the inner membrane of the nucleus (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data in Figure 1F.

claim: ER-FlucDM-mCherry aggregates in interphase cells possess minimal turnover.
source: In interphase cells, ER-FlucDM-mCherry aggregates intensity barely recovered after 4.5 min post-bleaching, indicating that ER-FlucDM-mCherry aggregates possessed minimal turnover similar to that of other protein aggregates such as Z-α1-antitrypsin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data in Figure 2A showing minimal recovery after photobleaching.

claim: ER-HaloDM-eGFP aggregates in the nucleus display low recovery after photobleaching.
source: Similarly, ER-HaloDM-eGFP aggregates in the nucleus also displayed low recovery after photobleaching (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ER-FlucDM-mCherry aggregates in mitotic cells show higher recovery than in interphase cells.
source: However, ER-FlucDM-mCherry aggregates in mitotic cells showed a higher recovery than that of in interphase cells (Figure 2D; aggregates of interphase cells recovered from 0.131±0.093–0.157±0.095; aggregates of mitotic cells recovered from 0.196±0.137–0.356±0.151).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP quantification data in Figure 2D showing statistically significant differences.

claim: The number and area of aggregates in telophase and early G1 cells are significantly lower than in interphase cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the number and area of aggregates in telophase and early G1 cells were significantly lower than in interphase cells, suggesting that aggregates are cleared gradually when cells progress through mitosis and cytokinesis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fixed cells at different cell cycle stages in Figure 3B.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates are released from the nucleus during nuclear envelope breakdown.
source: We observed that upon entry into mitosis, the ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates were released from the nucleus during nuclear envelope breakdown and gradually decreased in numbers as cells progress through mitosis and cytokinesis (Figure 3C and Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3C and Videos 1–3.

claim: In majority of early divided G1 cells, there are essentially no detectable aggregates.
source: In majority of early divided G1 cells, there was essentially no detectable aggregates (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3D.

claim: ER-HaloDM-eGFP aggregates decrease in numbers when cells progress through mitosis and cytokinesis.
source: Furthermore, aggregates formed in cells expressing ER-HaloDM-eGFP decreased in numbers when cells progress through mitosis and cytokinesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Video 2), suggesting that the clearance of protein aggregates during cell division was not specific to ER-FlucDM-eGFP.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Video 2.

claim: Gene expression for chaperones and co-chaperones in the ER are upregulated in cells expressing ER-FlucDM-eGFP.
source: Consistently, we observed that gene expression for chaperones and co-chaperones in the ER were upregulated in these cells (Figure 4A), indicating cells involved in ER proteostasis control during adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4A showing increased expression of ER chaperones.

claim: Proteomic analysis of cells expressing ER-FlucDM-GFP showed up-regulation of proteins involved in ER stress response.
source: Proteomic analysis of cells expressing ER-FlucDM-GFP showed up-regulation of proteins involved in ER stress response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Acute treatment with thapsigargin prevents clearance of ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates in dividing cells.
source: However, in cells at the late stage of cell division (65 min after release), there were significantly higher number of aggregates retained in the cytosol of Thaps-treated cells than in DMSO (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by fixed cell imaging and quantification in Figure 4B and C, and time-lapse imaging in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Prolonged pretreatment with tunicamycin prior to mitosis promotes aggregate clearance in dividing cells.
source: Interestingly, prolonged pretreatment of Tuni prior to mitosis promoted aggregate clearance in dividing cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C showing reduced aggregates with tunicamycin pretreatment.

claim: VER-155008 treatment prevents clearance of ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates in dividing cells.
source: We found that VER-treated dividing cells fixed after 65 min released from the G2/M boundary retained a high number of ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates in the cytosol compared to control treatment (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by fixed cell imaging and quantification in Figure 5A and B, and time-lapse imaging in Figure 5C.

claim: Inhibition of BiP's ATPase activity by YUM-70 leads to dose-dependent accumulation of ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates.
source: Similar to VER treatment, inhibition of BiP's ATPase activity by YUM-70 (Samanta et al., 2021) led to a dose-dependent accumulation of ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates in cells (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in Figure 5D and E showing increased aggregates with increasing YUM-70 concentration.

claim: BiP colocalizes with ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates.
source: Moreover, by using immunofluorescence staining, we found a strong colocalization of BiP and ER-FlucDM-eGFP, consistent with a role of BiP in regulating ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Proteasome inhibition with MG132 leads to accumulation of aggregates in metaphase-arrested cells.
source: After treating cells released from the G2/M boundary with low or high concentrations of MG132 for 55 min, majority of mitotic cells were arrested at metaphase and accumulated a high number of aggregates as compared to control cells treated with DMSO (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Proteasome inhibition in cells at late anaphase or telophase leads to accumulation of aggregates in early divided cells.
source: In cells completing cytokinesis, there were significantly high number of aggregates in the early divided cells treated with MG132 versus the control (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, G and H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, G and H.

claim: Cdk1 inhibition in MG132-arrested metaphase cells leads to clearance of ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates.
source: Interestingly, ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates were cleared in cells treated with RO-3306 while the aggregates were retained in cells treated with DMSO (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by fixed cell imaging and quantification in Figure 6A and B, and time-lapse imaging in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Inhibition of APC/C does not affect aggregate clearance in dividing cells.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of APC/C did not affect aggregate clearance as APC/Ci-treated cells that have arrested at metaphase have a comparable number of aggregates as in control DMSO-treated cells (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 6E and F showing no significant difference in aggregate numbers with APC/C inhibition.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP does not show a significant change in abundance after cycloheximide treatment.
source: ER-FlucDM-eGFP did not show a significant change in its abundance after CHX treatment, suggesting that ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates were not cleared by the protein degradation mechanism directly (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by protein blotting data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C.

claim: There is no significant change in GFP fluorescence intensity between early and late dividing cells.
source: Consistently, when the total GFP intensity of ER-FlucDM-eGFP was quantitated in dividing cells 20–30 min (early) or 85–95 min (late) released from G2/M boundary, there was no significant change in GFP fluorescence intensity between early and late dividing cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D), further supported that the protein degradation mechanism was not responsible for the ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregate clearance.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of total GFP intensity in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Depletion of ATL2 and ATL3 leads to accumulation of ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates in dividing cells.
source: Interestingly, dividing cells depleted of ATL2 and ATL3 accumulated more ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates than in control cells (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 7A and B showing increased aggregates after ATL2/ATL3 knockdown.

claim: Aurora A inhibition prevents aggregate clearance in mitotic cells.
source: When mitotic cells expressing ER-FlucDM-eGFP were treated with Aurora A inhibitor, MLN-8237, aggregate clearance was prevented compared to cells treated with DMSO (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 7C and D showing increased aggregates with MLN-8237 treatment.

claim: The proteome of mitotic cells has higher structural stability and is less aggregation-prone compared to interphase cells.
source: Previous studies showed that the proteome of mitotic cells has higher structural stability and is less aggregation-prone compared to that of in interphase cells (Becher et al., 2018; Wirth et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Becher et al., 2018 and Wirth et al., 2013.

claim: Post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation of mitotic proteins are suggested to be responsible for protein stability during cell division.
source: Post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation of mitotic proteins are suggested to be responsible for the protein stability during cell division (Becher et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Becher et al., 2018.

claim: The size of protein aggregates is limited by the ER tubules.
source: A previous study showed that the size of protein aggregates is limited by the ER tubules (Parashar et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Parashar et al., 2021.

claim: BiP translocates into the nucleus under stress.
source: These intranuclear membranous structures contain ER membranes and BiP, which is a key Hsp70 family chaperone in the ER and translocates into the nucleus under stress (Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2023.

claim: Aggregates are asymmetrically retained in one of the daughter cells that are usually short-lived.
source: It has been reported that aggregates are asymmetrically retained in one of the daughter cells that are usually short-lived (Rujano et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rujano et al., 2006.

claim: BiP solubilizes aggregates and drives aggregate clearance in the ER.
source: A recent study showed that BiP solubilizes aggregates and drives aggregate clearance in the ER (Melo et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Melo et al., 2022.

claim: Aggregate clearance is promoted by treating cells with ER stressors as the treatment triggers UPR, which leads to higher activity of BiP.
source: Interestingly, Melo et al. showed that aggregate clearance is promoted by treating ER-cells with ER stressors as the treatment triggers UPR, which in turn leads to higher activity of BiP to cope with the ER stress.
evidence: This statement is based on inference from the cited work of Melo et al.

claim: Mitotic cells are not very transcriptionally active.
source: It is possible that acute treatment of the ER stressor on dividing cells does not provide sufficient time for cells to accumulate abundant amount of BiP given that mitotic cells are not very transcriptionally active (Palozola et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Palozola et al., 2017.

claim: Degradation of BiP could be accelerated upon treatment of ER stressors.
source: Also, degradation of BiP could be accelerated upon the treatment of ER stressors, which in turn undermines the abundance of BiP in disaggregation (Shim et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shim et al., 2018.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates released from the nucleus during mitosis are still surrounded by the ER membrane.
source: Interestingly, the aggregates released from the nucleus during mitosis were still surrounded by the ER membrane as indicated by the ER-tracker (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and TEM data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Expression of CFTR-ΔF508 and AAT S or Z variants did not result in aggregate accumulation in the nucleus.
source: However, expression of CFTR-Δ508 and AAT S or Z variants did not result in the aggregate accumulation in the nucleus as observed in ER-FlucDM-eGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates may derive from the invagination of the inner nuclear membrane.
source: ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates may derive from the invagination of the inner nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that aggregates are surrounded by ER membrane in the nucleus.

claim: Morris et al., 1997 reported similar aggregate formation in the nucleus upon BiP overexpression.
source: Morris et al., 1997 reported a similar aggregate formation in the nucleus upon BiP overexpression.
evidence: This statement references a previous study by Morris et al., 1997.

claim: Aggregate clearance could represent an active mechanism that increases proteome stability in dividing cells.
source: The aggregate clearance we identified in this study could represent an active mechanism that increases proteome stability in dividing cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: APC/C targets mostly cytosolic proteins whereas ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates are confined in a membrane during mitosis.
source: It is possible that APC/C targets mostly cytosolic proteins whereas ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregates are confined in a membrane during mitosis.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why APC/C inhibition does not affect aggregate clearance.

claim: The confinement and clearance of protein aggregates during cell division presumably protect dividing cells from harmful effects of protein misfolding and aggregation.
source: The confinement and clearance of protein aggregates during cell division presumably protect dividing cells from harmful effects of protein misfolding and aggregation and ensure reliable inheritance of genetic materials.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the biological significance of the findings.

claim: Higher proteostatic stress renders cells more sensitive to perturbation of protein expression at the proteome level.
source: It is possible that higher proteostatic stress renders cells more sensitive to perturbation of the protein expression at the proteome level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the proteomic analysis findings.

claim: Changes in cell cycle protein levels may affect cell cycle transition and result in longer or shorter timeframes in certain cell cycle phases.
source: Changes in cell cycle protein levels may affect the cell cycle transition and result in longer or shorter timeframes in certain cell cycle phases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences of altered protein expression.

claim: Players involved in ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregate clearance are regulated by proteasomal degradation.
source: It is possible that players involved in ER-FlucDM-eGFP aggregate clearance are regulated by proteasomal degradation, which are affected when proteasomes are inhibited.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the role of proteasomes in aggregate clearance.

claim: Acute treatment of ER stressor on dividing cells does not provide sufficient time for cells to accumulate abundant BiP.
source: It is possible that acute treatment of the ER stressor on dividing cells does not provide sufficient time for cells to accumulate abundant amount of BiP given that mitotic cells are not very transcriptionally active (Palozola et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation combining citation and inference.

claim: BiP might function as a disaggregase to disassemble ER-FlucDM-eGFP when cells exit mitosis.
source: Also, BiP might function as a disaggregase to disassemble the ER-FlucDM-eGFP when cells exit mitosis.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Proteins involved in ER reorganization are regulated through protein modifications or proteasomal degradation to promote aggregate clearance in cell division.
source: While the molecular mechanism by which the ER-FlucDM-eGFP is cleared during mitosis and cytokinesis remains to be elucidated, we favor a model in which proteins involved in the ER reorganization are regulated through protein modifications or proteasomal degradation to promote aggregate clearance in cell division.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors.
